global-economics-e346a700b3.headline: Billionaire Mukesh Ambani launches India’s biggest-ever IPO
global-economics-e346a700b3.fulltext:
India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.
Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.
Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.
Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.
On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.
Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.
The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.
At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.
However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.
It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.
Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.
Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.
“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”

ai-9ea810a533.headline: Anthropic’s cloud partnerships are getting messy
ai-9ea810a533.fulltext:
Anthropic is having trouble securing enough cloud capacity from AWS, Google, and Microsoft, which increasingly see the Claude-maker as a competitor rather than a customer, according to an S-1 filing leaked to The Wall Street Journal.
The leaked filing provides more color to the numbers Reuters and the Financial Times reported in late September, including that Anthropic believes it could spend more $750 billion on cloud contracts, some of which includes deals still in negotiation.
And still, that is not enough. Anthropic is leasing its own data centers and working with third-party data center operators. But the firm worries those operators have a “limited operating history,” which could make them less reliable than the hyperscalers.
Anthropic’s enormous spend comes on the back of an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of the year. The company reported $16.3 billion in revenue during that same time period, with only two customers accounting for about a fifth of sales, according to the WSJ report.
Building on previously reported catastrophic risk disclosures, the filing also warns that Anthropic could be held liable for damages caused by harmful AI behavior to a tune that would exceed available insurance coverage.
Last week, the company told prospective investors that third-quarter revenue alone has now reached $16.8 billion, up 45% from the previous quarter. Anthropic is reportedly targeting a November IPO.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

ai-5ecb5ba802.headline: US bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agencies
ai-5ecb5ba802.fulltext:
The US government on Monday ordered its agencies to stop using artificial intelligence (AI) tools from the Chinese startup DeepSeek, as the countries race for dominance in the fast-moving sector.
A notice from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced the ban on products developed by DeepSeek – and tools created using DeepSeek by third parties – saying they must be removed from IT devices.
The DHS can issue direction to civilian agencies but not the military or intelligence services. The US defense department did not respond to an AFP request for comment.
“DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” said a document attached to Monday’s notice.
Use of DeepSeek AI tools “may result in the transfer of sensitive data to [China] if used by US government employees or vendors”, the department warned.
Its servers are located in China, where the legal system permits the government “extensive authority” to access private company infrastructure, it said.
DeepSeek has been contacted for comment.
One of China’s top AI labs, DeepSeek shook up the industry in January 2025 with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, challenging assumptions of US dominance.
The firm released a long-awaited new model, V4, in April, and earlier in October updated a faster, more lightweight version of V4.
The US has accused DeepSeek and other top Chinese AI firms of systematically stealing the capabilities of cutting-edge models developed by American rivals.
Despite their fierce competition in the field, when their leaders Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met at the White House in September, China and the US agreed to set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents.
The topic is expected to arise again at a meeting between Xi and Trump at a summit scheduled for November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

deep-tech-b700c37a12.headline: L&T Semiconductor, Tata Electronics Partner on Chip Manufacturing in India
deep-tech-b700c37a12.fulltext:
The partnership will evaluate fabrication and packaging options for L&T Semiconductor products, including design-to-manufacturing optimization.
L&T Semiconductor Technologies Ltd (LTSCT) and Tata Electronics have agreed to explore semiconductor fabrication and packaging opportunities in India, combining L&T’s chip design capabilities with Tata Electronics’ foundry and packaging operations.
The companies will assess manufacturing options for L&T Semiconductor’s existing and future products across Tata Electronics’ fabrication processes and packaging technologies. The work will also cover design-to-fabrication optimization to improve manufacturing efficiency at scale.
The collaboration targets products for automotive, industrial, communications, security and intelligent-edge applications, with the companies seeking to build domestic design and manufacturing capabilities for Indian and global markets.
“Semiconductor leadership will increasingly be defined not just by design breakthroughs but by the ability to industrialise those designs through advanced packaging and manufacturing. At LTSCT, we see this as India’s opportunity to move up the value chain. Our engagement with Tata Electronics is a decisive step in building those capabilities, ensuring that the next generation of semiconductor products can be designed in India and delivered to global markets with speed, reliability and scale,” said Dr. Sandeep Kumar, Chief Executive, L&T Semiconductor.
Tata Electronics CEO and Managing Director Dr. Randhir Thakur said the partnership combines L&T Semiconductor’s design and engineering expertise with Tata Electronics’ manufacturing, packaging and testing capabilities.
“Tata Electronics is establishing world‑class semiconductor manufacturing capabilities in India to provide trusted, high-quality solutions across the semiconductor value chain to our domestic and global customers. Our partnership with LTSCT is a significant step which will accelerate India’s vision of becoming a full-stack semiconductor nation, by combining L&T Semiconductor’s deep fabless design and engineering expertise with our capabilities across semiconductor manufacturing, packaging and testing,” he added.
The agreement supports India’s efforts to expand its domestic semiconductor ecosystem under the government’s Manufacture in India – for India and for the World initiative. The companies also plan to work on packaging technologies, manufacturing processes and quality systems.

global-economics-9206eb147f.headline: Crash! KOSPI in free fall? South Korea stock market down another 5%, tanks 40% from record high- What’s driving AI rout?
global-economics-9206eb147f.fulltext:
Pranati DevaPublished20 Oct 2026, 02:53 PM IST South Korea’s stock market is facing a deepening sell-off as concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) spending, semiconductor valuations and rising financing costs rattle investors. The benchmark KOSPI fell another 5% on Tuesday, extending its losses as investors pulled back from AI-linked stocks. The index had surged earlier this year, with its gains reaching around 116% at its record close in June. However, the subsequent correction has erased much of that rally, leaving the KOSPI up approximately 30% in 2026. The index has also fallen 39% from its peak of 9,386 earlier this year to 5,493.24 currently. The sell-off accelerated in July, when the KOSPI fell 22%, and continued into October, with the index losing another 17% through October 16. The latest pressure has been particularly severe for semiconductor stocks, which account for a significant share of South Korea’s market. SK Hynix shares have plunged around 35% from their peak, while Samsung Electronics has fallen approximately 22%. The weakness has spread to newer AI-linked businesses, too, with data-centre infrastructure company Elice Inc. dropping as much as 32% during its trading debut in Seoul. The latest decline follows a global sell-off in AI and semiconductor stocks that wiped out more than $1 trillion in market value from 20 of the world’s most valuable AI and semiconductor companies last week. South Korea has been particularly vulnerable because of its heavy dependence on Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Together, the two companies accounted for 44% of the KOSPI in May. As a result, a sharp decline in either stock can have a significant impact on the broader index. Stronger-than-expected US inflation data has added to the uncertainty. Hotter inflation can reduce the likelihood of interest-rate cuts and revive expectations of rate hikes, raising borrowing costs and putting pressure on highly valued growth stocks. According to a Reuters report, OpenAI told investors last week that its annualised revenue for September was nearly $50 billion, below a figure it had indicated earlier. At a separate event, the company had previously said its September revenue run rate was approaching $70 billion. The discrepancy reportedly stemmed largely from an effort to compare its revenue directly with that of rival Anthropic. Concerns about funding are also emerging from within the semiconductor industry. Earlier this week, Broadcom chief executive Hock Tan said capital could become a bigger constraint on AI expansion than shortages of semiconductors, memory chips or electricity. Daniel Munday, Principal Analyst at VT Markets, said the combination of inflation concerns and doubts about AI financing had intensified the sell-off across Asian markets. “Hotter US CPI revived Fed hike bets, then cautious Fed comments pulled them back. At the same time, AI financing worries hit US tech, with CoreWeave and Oracle sold off on debt fears. Asia took the hit, and the KOSPI closed down 7.57%, its seventh straight loss, with foreign investors heavy sellers,” Munday said. Munday also noted that US Treasury yields and the dollar eased overnight as investors sought safer assets. A Bloomberg report suggesting China held more US debt than official data showed also influenced market sentiment. The sell-off has intensified the debate over whether AI stocks can sustain their earnings growth and justify their valuations. Some analysts believe investors may need to diversify beyond the sector rather than remain heavily exposed to the AI trade. In his latest GREED & fear note, Jefferies Global Head of Equity Strategy Chris Wood highlighted a warning from the brokerage’s global quantitative strategy team that “it has become time to diversify beyond AI.” The report projects earnings growth for global AI stocks to slow from nearly 100% in 2026 to 30% in 2027 and 22% in 2028. By comparison, earnings growth for global stocks excluding AI is expected to decline from 16% in 2026 to 9% in both 2027 and 2028. Wood has also highlighted rising borrowing costs as a central factor in the AI spending boom, raising questions about how long companies and investors can sustain the current pace of investment. Munday said a rebound was possible after such a rapid fall, especially as US yields and the dollar eased. However, he cautioned that markets with heavy semiconductor exposure, including South Korea, Taiwan and Japan, could remain volatile until concerns about AI spending and interest rates subside. Investors will be watching the US Federal Reserve’s October 28 meeting, further inflation data, oil prices and tensions in the Middle East. india-93bb3b248d.headline: China cites security reasons to restrict export of key machinery used in India's infrastructure development
india-93bb3b248d.fulltext:
(TibetanReview.net, Oct20’26) – After previously preventing a German company from exporting tunnel boring machines manufactured especially for India from its factories in China, Beijing has announced new export controls on such machines and related vital items. Such machines are critically needed in India for its metro, highway, and other major infrastructure projects.
These restrictions will take effect on Nov 18 and apply to tunnel boring machines and related items, reported PTI news agency Oct 19. Additionally, the export controls include critically important walking excavators and specific dredger-related items, complicating several Indian projects.
China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) has said the restrictions were aimed at safeguarding national security and interests.
The restrictions could affect several projects in India, including underground metro systems, high-speed rail lines and tunnels in various locations, including border areas.
In 2024, India’s Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal told German Vice Chancellor Robert Habeck that Beijing was not allowing a German company manufacturing TBMs in China to export them to India.
Announced as a part of new export restrictions affecting 14 technologies spanning sectors from artificial intelligence (AI) and biotechnology to photovoltaic solar power, exporters of the relevant items must apply for licences from MOFCOM in accordance with China’s Export Control Law and Regulations on Export Control of Dual-Use Items.
The latest restrictions come a year after a German tunnel boring machine manufacturer faced difficulties exporting equipment from its factories in China to India, noted businesstoday.in Oct 19.
It said that in Sep 2025, Germany’s Ambassador to India, Philipp Ackermann, revealed that Chinese customs had blocked at least three tunnel boring machines manufactured by German company Herrenknecht and destined for Indian infrastructure projects.
Ackermann suggested that the delays were for political reasons. “The tunnel boring machines is an interesting case: So it is clear for political reasons that the Chinese would not really let them out. Now they are out…They are coming in. I think one came a month ago…The last one is coming now.”
The machines had been manufactured at Herrenknecht’s facilities in China for export to India but became caught up in restrictions amid tensions between New Delhi and Beijing after the 2020 Galwan clashes, the report said.
Following the export disruptions, Herrenknecht was stated to have decided to establish production facilities in India to reduce its dependence on Chinese manufacturing operations.
“Of course the company says that it cannot do business when Chinese customs are not allowing this. They are now setting up shop in India, they are trying to produce here. It is a good example on how to diversify, do not put your eggs in one basket only,” Ackermann was quoted as saying.

india-f5c2c4af86.headline: India-New Zealand FTA comes into force; new visa categories for Indians, zero-duty access for exports
india-f5c2c4af86.fulltext:
India’s free trade agreement with New Zealand came into force on Tuesday (October 20, 2026), eliminating 100% tariffs on Indian exports to the country and introducing $20 billion worth of foreign direct investment into India as part of the deal. Moreover, 95% of New Zealand’s exports to India will either be allowed tariff-free or at “sharply” reduced levies.
The FTA was signed on April 27 in New Delhi and ratified on September 21. New Zealand’s Parliament, on September 16, had passed legislation to implement the FTA.
EDITORIAL | Trading smart: On the India-New Zealand FTA
According to the New Zealand government’s immigration department, the new FTA brings with it new visa commitments for the country.
“The FTA includes two new Temporary Employment Entry (TEE) visa categories, expanded post-study work rights for some Indian graduates, commitments around in-study work rights for Indian students, and a new working holiday scheme,” the Immigration department said in a statement.
“The new TEE visa pathways available from 20 October 2026 are for highly skilled occupations and a small number of professions considered iconic to India.”
“These allow up to 5,000 TEE visa holders in New Zealand at any one time, with most places allocated to skilled occupations already identified on New Zealand’s Green List.”
Gains for India
New Zealand is giving 100% duty-free market access to Indian exporters from Tuesday (October 20, 2026). It covers all tariff lines or product categories and 100% of India’s current exports to New Zealand.
This is the first FTA for India where it receives full duty-free access across all tariff lines from entering into force.
Eliminating import duty would remove the tariff disadvantage of pre-FTA rates, up to 10%, that Indian exporters face in the New Zealand market.
The major sectors that would benefit include fruits and vegetables; coffee, tea, cocoa and spices; cereals; processed foods; textiles and clothing; leather and footwear; pharmaceuticals; engineering goods; marine products; plastics and rubber.
Gains for New Zealand
India is giving tariff concessions on 70% of its tariff lines, covering about 95% of the current bilateral trade value. The remaining 29.97% of the lines have been kept in the exclusion list.
India is giving duty-based quota for apples, kiwifruit, manuka honey and albumins, along with minimum import price (MIP) provisions and other safeguard measures.
This approach is expected to ensure calibrated imports while protecting the interests of domestic farmers.

ai-a323e283c5.headline: OpenAI acquires startup Orchestra Bio⁠ to beef up its biotech business
ai-a323e283c5.fulltext:
OpenAI on Tuesday acquired a four-year-old AI biotech software startup called Orchestra Bio, the company announced via its website. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the startup had reportedly raised around $20 million as of 2025 from backers like Andreessen Horowitz, Atria, and 8VC.
Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials.
OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind, its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results. OpenAI has already won some big names as customers for Rosalind, including, it says, Moderna and Novo Nordisk.
The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma. In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors. In this case, Orchestra is getting absorbed, rather than stomped out.

ai-f5c5b586cf.headline: Infrastructure startup Fireworks AI is in early talks for new funding at a valuation between $30 billion and $40 billion
ai-f5c5b586cf.fulltext:
Fireworks AI is seeking to raise fresh funding at a valuation between $30 billion and $40 billion, a dramatic jump just months after the AI-infrastructure startup was valued at $17.5 billion, according to people familiar with the matter.
The potential valuation leap reflects investors' appetite for the companies selling the computing power and tools fueling the AI boom, even as Fireworks AI works through the fallout from a recent security incident.
The talks around the financing are still early, and valuation targets could still change. Fireworks declined to comment.
Founded in 2022, Fireworks was built by veterans of Meta and Google's AI efforts. Chief executive Lin Qiao previously led the PyTorch team at Meta, while cofounders include former Meta infrastructure engineers and a former leader of Google's Vertex AI. The company rents out computing infrastructure and software that lets businesses run, fine-tune, and deploy open-weight and custom AI models.
In July, Fireworks announced a $1.5 billion Series D funding round at a $17.5 billion valuation, led by Atreides Management, Index Ventures, and TCV, with participation from Nvidia, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Menlo Ventures. That round followed a $250 million Series C at a $4 billion valuation in late 2025, co-led by Lightspeed, Index, and Evantic. Last month, The Information reported that Fireworks has been considering a round at a $30 billion.
Rather than trying to build a consumer chatbot to rival ChatGPT, Fireworks sells what it calls specialized intelligence: models customized on a customer's proprietary data, workflows, and use cases. The company said in July that it had surpassed $1 billion in annualized revenue and was serving more than 40 trillion tokens a day; it said 95% of those tokens came from models tailored to customers.
The company operates in a highly competitive layer of the AI stack. Rivals include model-infrastructure startups such as Together AI, Baseten, and Replicate, as well as cloud giants such as Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, and Oracle.
The fundraising talks come shortly after a security incident at Fireworks AI. The company said it identified unauthorized use of internal credentials earlier this month that allowed an intruder to access data from some customer accounts.
"We take this seriously and will be transparent about what happened and what we find," Qiao posted on X. "I'm personally committed to turn this attack into the most formidable security response in AI Infra."

deep-tech-a2b325808a.headline: OpenAI Plans Humanoid Robot Demo in 2027 as Hardware Push Expands
deep-tech-a2b325808a.fulltext:
OpenAI is building its own humanoid robots and expects to demonstrate an early prototype in 2027, pushing the ChatGPT maker deeper into physical AI and hardware.
Chief Executive Sam Altman confirmed the company’s robotics ambitions and said the first public demonstration could arrive next year.
But the 2027 target is not a commercial launch date.
OpenAI has not revealed what the robot will look like, how much it may cost or when machines could become available outside the company.
FCRF’s Chief AI Officer Certification Returns on November 14 to Prepare Future AI Leaders
OpenAI Wants AI to Move Into the Physical World
Altman has said OpenAI intends to build humanoid robots rather than limiting itself to AI models that operate through computers and phones.
The reasoning is practical.
Most workplaces and homes are designed around the human body.
Doors, stairs, tools, shelves and machines are positioned so people can interact with them using arms, hands and legs.
A humanoid robot could therefore operate in existing environments without requiring companies to redesign entire buildings around machines.
OpenAI is expected to initially focus on industrial tasks.
Reports say potential applications include work inside factories, facilities and data centres before the technology eventually moves into more general environments.
Altman has stressed that the hardest part is not simply building a machine with arms and legs.
The bigger challenge is developing the intelligence that allows a robot to understand what is happening around it and respond safely.
2027 Target Is a Demo, Not a Product Launch
Altman told Fortune that OpenAI expects to have an impressive robotics demonstration in 2027.
He also cautioned that humanoid robots operating widely in public spaces are likely to remain several years away.
That distinction matters.
A controlled demonstration can show that a robot can perform selected tasks under specific conditions.
A commercial machine has to work reliably for hours, deal with unexpected situations and operate safely around people.
It also has to survive mechanical wear, manage battery constraints and recover when something goes wrong.
OpenAI has not disclosed what capabilities its 2027 prototype will demonstrate.
The company has also not announced manufacturing partners or production targets.
For now, the timetable should therefore be viewed as an engineering milestone rather than a product-release commitment.
OpenAI Hiring Shows Hardware Ambitions Are Serious
OpenAI’s own recruitment activity provides stronger evidence that the robotics programme extends well beyond software research.
Its careers page currently lists 17 positions under its robotics team.
Roles include control-systems engineers, electrical engineers, robotics safety specialists and engineers responsible for motors and actuators.
Actuators are the mechanical systems that convert electronic commands into physical movement.
They allow a robot to bend joints, move limbs and manipulate objects.
OpenAI is also hiring specialists in manufacturing and supply chains.
That suggests the company is thinking beyond experimental AI models and building expertise in the actual physical components required for robots.
One OpenAI listing says its robotics team is developing general-purpose systems for dynamic real-world environments.
Another seeks engineers to design custom motors, gearboxes, sensors and testing systems.
The recruitment activity indicates OpenAI wants control over both the intelligence and at least significant parts of the robot hardware.
OpenAI Is Returning to Robotics After Earlier Research
Robotics is not entirely new for OpenAI.
The company previously operated a dedicated robotics research programme before later shutting it down.
One of its best-known projects was Dactyl, an AI system trained to control a robotic hand.
OpenAI demonstrated the system manipulating objects and later showed a robotic hand solving a Rubik’s Cube.
The research was notable because much of the training occurred inside simulations before being transferred to real hardware.
That technique remains important in modern robotics.
Training every physical movement on real machines can be slow, expensive and potentially dangerous.
Simulations allow AI systems to experience large numbers of scenarios before being deployed in the real world.
OpenAI is now returning to the field with much larger AI models and significantly more computing resources.
Humanoid Robotics Race Is Getting Crowded
OpenAI will enter a market already attracting major investment.
Tesla is developing its Optimus humanoid robot, initially targeting factory work.
Figure is also building general-purpose humanoids and has raised billions of dollars to expand development.
Other companies are pursuing robots for warehouses, manufacturing and household tasks.
OpenAI has previously invested in or worked with robotics companies, including Figure and 1X.
Developing its own machines could eventually put it in competition with companies it previously supported.
The biggest question will be whether OpenAI can transfer the capabilities of advanced AI models into reliable physical behaviour.
A chatbot can generate another answer after making a mistake.
A robot moving machinery or working beside a person cannot afford the same margin for error.
That makes safety, control systems and mechanical reliability just as important as intelligence.
What this means for you:
OpenAI’s move into humanoid robotics shows that advanced AI is beginning to move from software into physical machines. The 2027 target is only for a demonstration, however, and widespread commercial robots are still likely to take longer.

deep-tech-dc5abb9a41.headline: China creates state-owned firm in Xiongan to develop nation’s AI data resources

China has set up a new state-owned enterprise dedicated to managing the country’s massive data resources, a significant move designed to turbocharge the nation’s artificial intelligence industry and bolster its digital economy.
The National Data Group Co – based in China’s “city of the future”, Xiongan New Area in northern Hebei province – is tasked with “developing and utilising data resources, unlocking the value of data elements, serving AI development and fostering a data industry ecosystem”, according to a report by state news agency Xinhua.
Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang attended the company’s launch ceremony on Tuesday. Ding described the creation of the state-owned company as a “major strategic decision” made by the party leadership, led by President Xi Jinping.
The move was crucial for China to “seize the initiative in AI development, accelerate the construction of a ‘digital China’, and build new national competitive advantages”, Xinhua quoted Ding as saying.
The creation of the new company came as Xiongan, known for housing state-owned institutions relocated from Beijing, moves to nurture its own industries and attract technology firms, according to reporting by the South China Morning Post.
Officials were looking to attract tech companies that could reach valuations of 10 billion yuan (US$1.5 billion) and potentially list on major stock markets – including Hong Kong’s – over the next few years, according to sources. Key target sectors included AI, satellite internet and robotics, they added.

State-owned enterprises have anchored the first wave of arrivals. China Satellite Network Group and China Huaneng, a major power generation company, have moved their headquarters to Xiongan. deep-tech-a2da803db9.headline: Alibaba’s RISC-V IP powers over 6 billion shipped chips as tech giant targets AI, autos

Alibaba Group Holding’s research arm, Damo Academy, has seen more than 6 billion chips shipped based on its XuanTie RISC-V architecture, marking a milestone as the tech giant doubles down on the open standard in artificial intelligence and automotive systems.
Meng Jianyi, chief scientist at Damo Academy, announced the figure on Monday at the annual RISC-V Summit China in Shenzhen. The achievement comes as Chinese companies seek to play a greater role in the global RISC-V ecosystem, an alternative to established chip architectures developed by the likes of Intel and Arm.
Alibaba, based in Hangzhou, was an early mover in China’s RISC-V landscape and is expanding its AI infrastructure capabilities. Because the architecture is an open standard, developers can use it to design processors while potentially reducing reliance on foreign chip-design technologies amid US-led export restrictions.
Highlighting the architecture’s rapid global adoption, Meng cited forecasts from research firm Omdia that global RISC-V processor shipments would grow by nearly 30 per cent annually and could account for about 25 per cent of the worldwide processor market by 2030.
The shipment milestone follows the launch earlier this year of the XuanTie C950, a flagship RISC-V processor that Alibaba called the most powerful of its kind globally. The company said it was developed to support AI agents and other workloads in cloud and high-performance computing environments, and that it delivered more than three times the performance of its predecessor, the C920.
The C950 is part of a broader push by Chinese tech companies to develop the computing infrastructure needed for AI. Alibaba, Tencent Holdings and ByteDance are also competing to develop AI agents – software that can autonomously perform tasks on behalf of users or other systems – and integrate them into their apps.
RISC-V, short for fifth-generation reduced instruction set computer, is an open-standard instruction set architecture that allows developers to design central processing units (CPUs). It is managed by the non-profit RISC-V International.
Free for anyone to use and modify, RISC-V is considered a potential route for China to achieve greater self-sufficiency in chip design. The architecture offers designers an alternative to Intel’s x86 and Arm’s namesake architecture, which power devices running Microsoft Windows and Google Android, respectively.
Despite the progress, however, Meng highlighted the engineering challenges involved as Alibaba seeks to improve the performance of its RISC-V CPUs when running large language models.
“The biggest challenge lies in co-design,” Meng said in an interview with RISC-V International, released by the Damo Academy last week. “Isolated raw computing power means little; the key is balancing computation, data movement and software optimisation.”
For large AI models such as Qwen3.8-27B, he added, techniques such as quantisation, matrix instructions and memory bandwidth must be integrated as a unified system.

New Delhi: Indian small arms manufacturer SSS Defence and defence major Kalyani Group have been shortlisted as the Development cum Production Partners (DcPP) for an Armament Research and Development Establishment (ARDE) project to develop an indigenous 20 mm aviation gun and turret system, ThePrint has learnt.
The guns are intended for Hindustan Aeronautics Limited’s (HAL’s) Advanced Light Helicopter (ALH) Mk-IV, also known as Rudra, and Light Combat Helicopter (LCH) platforms. ARDE, a laboratory under the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), is responsible for designing and developing conventional armaments, ammunition and related systems. It works with public- and private-sector production agencies to translate weapon designs into systems deployable by the armed forces.
Sources said ARDE and HAL signed an MoU for collaboration last year, following which bidding was called. The bid was won by SSS Defence and Kalyani. The order will be split between them after the development stage, depending on the cost calculations.
It is expected that the development phase will take about two years and order will be given post the acceptance phase. The order will be split between them depending on cost calculations with the L1 getting 60 percent of the order and the other getting 40 percent.
This is the very first design and development of an aviation medium caliber gun to date in India.
The project is part of India’s broader push to indigenous critical weapon systems and reduce dependence on foreign suppliers.
The 20 mm turret gun is an important component of the weapon suite of armed helicopters, enabling them to engage ground targets in support of troops and during combat operations. The ALH Mk-IV, the weaponised version of HAL’s Dhruv helicopter, is designed to carry a range of weapons, including a 20 mm turret gun, 70 mm rocket pods and missiles.
The LCH Prachand, India’s indigenous attack helicopter, is also equipped with a 20 mm turret gun and 70 mm rockets, besides anti-tank guided missiles. The Indian Army has previously conducted firing trials of the LCH’s 20 mm turret gun, including during day and night operations.

Akriti AnandPublished20 Oct 2026, 03:13 PM IST Discovered Materials is a startup that builds AI "scientists" to discover new materials for the semiconductor industry. It is backed by a $9 million seed round led by Lightspeed, with participation from Y Combinator and Peak XV, and angels like Paul Graham, Gokul Rajaram and Thariq Shihipar. The San Francisco-based start-up is the latest, with plans to use swarms of AI agents to accelerate the discovery of semiconductor materials that could help address the growing problem of heat generated by powerful artificial intelligence (AI) chips. As interesting as the startup's mission sounds, even more spectacular is the profile of the co-founders of this million-dollar idea. Meet Advaith and Akash: Advaith Sridhar and Akash Ramdas are the co-founders of Discovered Material. The two met over 10 years ago at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Madras. Akash Ramdas earned a BTech degree in Metallurgical and Material Engineering, batch 2015-2019, from IIT Madras. He holds a Masters and a PhD in Material Science from Stanford University, and has spent the last 11 years researching new materials for semiconductor chips. Akash's work on new nanoscale interconnects was Stanford Engineering’s most popular story of 2025, as per their profile on his start-up's website. startup Following his doctorate, Ramdas worked as a postdoctoral researcher at Stanford from September 2025 to April 2026. Before joining Stanford, Akash worked as a Programme Manager, healthcare at The ePlane company, where he was involved in "customising aerial vehicles to deliver medicines and medical products faster," according to his LinkedIn profile. He co-founded Discovered Material with Advaith in March 2026. Advaith Sridhar studied AI at Carnegie Mellon and was a research engineer building video models and agents at Persona AI (acquired) and Luma Labs. Sridhar was awarded the best outgoing student of the IIT Madras batch graduation in 2019, according to his LinkedIn profile. Previously, Sridhar worked as a product manager at Flipkart and later at Turing.com. As a project lead at AI4Bharat, he "published India's first sign language video dataset and models." He was the founding AI Engineer at Persona AI (acquired by Luma). To put it simply, chips running AI workloads are too hot. That’s one reason why data centres consume so much electricity and require cooling systems. And now, entrepreneurs are turning to AI to solve the problem it created. Founders Advaith Sridhar and Akash Ramdas teamed up to launch the company, drawing on Ramdas’ experience earning a doctorate in materials science from Stanford, and Sridhar’s work on agents at Persona AI and Luma Labs. Discovered Materials aims to use AI agents, computational modelling, and laboratory testing to help researchers identify promising semiconductor materials more quickly, according to a report by TechCrunch. The AI agents come up with candidates, simulate them, and then the candidates are built and tested in real labs, a person who identified himself as Advaith's colleague at Turing explained on LinkedIn. The start-up is also releasing Material Discovery Bench, an open-source benchmark for AI-driven materials discovery. In a brief published on the company's website, Discovered Materials acknowledged that AI chips have a major heat problem — which is limiting every AI data centre right now. "GPUs today handle heat fluxes of ~140 W/cm², higher than a space shuttle nose cone re-entering the earth’s atmosphere, with each generation generating more heat than the last. This heat is why datacenters consume so much power and water; they need it to stay cool during operation," the company noted. It added that the amount of heat produced by a chip and the speed at which it dissipates are both influenced by the materials used to make it. "Today’s materials are at their limit, and new materials can improve chips by orders of magnitude. However, discovering a new material and getting it into a fab takes years and hundreds of millions of dollars. Most ideas die in this valley of death, between a science experiment and a fab," the company said. According to TechCrunch, the two have created a software pipeline that uses Anthropic models in a custom harness to generate material leads, and then turns to foundational physics models they’ve trained to run simulations that verify if the candidate materials are actually of interest. “[Ramdas] was doing maybe 20 guesses a day during his PhD,” Sridhar told TechCrunch. "We’re able to do thousands of guesses a day now by having these agents run 24/7 on the cloud, exploring research directions that he gives them," he added. indian-startups-15d8f31b97.headline: FSSAI Crackdown Continues With Fresh Show-Cause Notices Issued To Zepto, Others
indian-startups-15d8f31b97.fulltext: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has issued show-cause notices to quick commerce unicorn Zepto as well as several food and nutraceutical brands amid a broader crackdown on food safety violations. The notice against Zepto followed a consumer complaint on social media alleging delivery of expired packets of besan (gram flour). The regulator directed the platform to submit order logs, seller details, warehouse tracking, root-cause analysis, and proof of stock withdrawal and customer refunds. Besides Zepto, nutraceutical brands BMS Lifescience and HealthyHey Foods, as well as bakery brand Bakelite Food Processing, received show-cause notices over misleading labelling and advertising. Bakelite: The parent company behind Pune-based Malpani Foods was targeted over describing its product, ‘Malpani’s Bakelite Puneri Cream Roll’, as ‘creamy’. However, the product includes no cream or any other dairy-based ingredients but hydrogenated vegetable fat, margarine, and sugar. BMS Lifescience: The brand was marketing ‘HAOG’s Cranberry Urinary Tract Health Capsules’ under an expired FSSAI registration certificate, and also made health-related claims around disease risk reduction pertaining to the kidney and urinary tract without approval from the regulator. It was also pulled up for misleading usage of the official FSSAI logo, non-compliant use of the claim “as directed by healthcare practitioner”, and making potentially misleading claims online. HealthyHey Foods: The regulator called out the brand for discrepancies in labelled ingredients across its website and Flipkart regarding its “HealthyHey Nutrition Natural Cranberry Extract 25% Capsules”. It further alleged the brand was making unapproved claims like “100% Natural”; and marketing the product with the FSSAI logo and “FSSAI certified” in a misleading way. The regulator has directed all the companies to submit comprehensive written explanations and corrective action reports within stipulated deadlines or face license suspensions and statutory penalties. Just days earlier, the regulator pulled up BigBasket and Flipkart over misleading promotions carried by products sold on the respective platforms. Besides, the FSSAI has also sanctioned adjudication proceedings against beverage brand Storia. It had earlier flagged the brand’s pomegranate juice for containing only 4% pomegranate juice concentrate and 12% apple juice concentrate, in spite of misleading front-of-pack branding and visual imagery. The authority had also cited non-compliant declarations, including prominent “No Added Sugar” claims alongside obscured disclosures, and the unapproved claim “Equivalent to 100% Fruit Juice (Reconstituted)”. Notably, the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) had also fined the brand ₹1 Lakh for misleading consumers. The consumer protection body pulled up Storia for using the branding “100%” in their product labelling, due to reconstituted ingredients and lack of evidence. The latest series of notices fits into a larger pattern of the FSSAI identifying illegal food labelling and marketing practices on products sold online. Till now, it has also penalised multiple platforms — Amazon, Bigbasket, Flipkart, Swiggy Instamart and Zepto — for allegedly engaging in misbranding, misleading claims, and sale and display of prohibited or poisonous food articles. For Zepto, the fresh regulatory scrutiny adds on to legal issues the quick commerce major has been facing ahead of its proposed public plans. Zepto disclosed multiple ongoing regulatory and labour-related proceedings in its updated DRHP, which was filed with the markets regulator SEBI earlier in June. These include consumer protection cases over alleged dark patterns, food safety violations as well as an Enforcement Directorate inquiry into its ownership structure under FEMA. The company’s subsidiary has also faced allegations of overcharging beyond MRP and misleading advertisements. Other pending matters involve alleged wage underpayment, trade licence violations and food safety issues across several states. Besides the regulatory challenges, Zepto had faced unalignment with institutional investors over its IPO valuations which led the company to pause its IPO until May 2027. The quick commerce major is currently chasing a pre-IPO placement of about ₹1,000 Cr.

climate-energy-cd462dfd70.headline: India curtails 96.9GW of solar PV in September
climate-energy-cd462dfd70.fulltext:
Curtailment was four times higher between May and August 2026 than in the same period in the previous year. Image: Sunsure Energy.
Research and analysis company JMK has released a report on curtailment of renewable energy generation in India, showing that solar PV curtailment reached 96.9GW in September.
While curtailment in September this year was lower than the previous year’s figure, down 24%, this follows a period between May and August in which curtailment was four times higher compared to the same period in 2025.
In September 2026, the equivalent of 1.28% (118.6GW) of total renewable energy was curtailed, with solar comprising 96.9GW of curtailment, and the majority of the remainder comprising wind generation. JMK suggests that the reasons for renewable curtailment include demand-generation mismatches, transmission constraints and a lack of storage and grid flexibility.
Seasonal trends can also affect curtailment figures. JMK considers the period from April to July to be the peak window of renewable generation in India, while autumn can be characterised by high renewable output and moderate electricity demand, leading to higher curtailment.
According to JM figures, October 2025 saw the highest rate of curtailment since May 2025, with 4.32% of generation curtailed, as shown in the graph below.
October 2025 saw the highest monthly VRE curtailment, as a percentage of total generation, of 4.32%. Image: JMK.
Grid-India divides variable renewable energy (VRE) curtailment into two categories: Real-time system constraints, where back-down instructions are issued on any particular day in order to manage congestion and operating limits; and emergency Tertiary Reserve Ancillary Service (TRAS) Down orders. The latter involves reducing generation to balance supply and demand and indicates the power system is unable to accommodate the power from available renewables.
Of September’s curtailment, 146.73MUs (39%) was due to real-time system constraints and 231.79MUs (61%) was due to Emergency TRAS Down in VRE, of which solar accounted for 82%. JMK suggests that September’s figures were “driven mainly by the need to balance the power system, rather than by grid congestion alone.”
Gujarat and Rajasthan generated 79% of curtailed energy in September, with Rajasthan’s curtailment (29.1% of the total) entirely affecting solar projects, as shown in the diagram below.
The western states of Gujarat and Rajasthan generated 79% of India’s curtailed energy in September. Image: JMK.
While JMK notes thatcurtailment fell from August to September this year, the analyst frames this as “seasonal relief rather than evidence of a structural improvement in grid integration.”
Indeed, JMK notes that further deployment of battery energy storage systems (BESS) could “reduce curtailment” in the long-term, but notes that BESS projects would have had to provide an average of 12.6 GWh per day in September to obviate curtailment. This figure that equates to 3GW of 4-hour storage capacity.
JMK calls for prioritisation of nodes in Gujarat and Rasjasthan needing storage sized to recurring surpluses in order to help absorb TRAS Down events. Such storage would be able to complement transmission upgrades and improve forecasting for flexible markets, the report states.
The need for seasonal and location-specific curtailment will be increased by further renewable energy installations, reads the report, which adds that addition of around 44.6GW of solar generation in FY2026 has increased pressure on transmission infrastructure and grid flexibility.
While Indian solar PV additions in Q2 2026 were 43% lower than in the previous quarter, JMK figures released earlier this year show that utility-scale solar additions in India rose 32% between H1 2025 and H1 2026.
Accommodating these renewable energy capacity additions will require more investments in India’s transmission infrastructure, according to Indian credit rating agency ICRA, which estimated that the country will need to add around 20,000 circuit kilometres of transmission lines and 120 gigavolt-amperes of substation capacity every year for five years to meet the Indian government’s National Electricity Plan-II targets. India is expected to spend IN5 trillion (US$52 billion) between 2027 and 2032 on its power transmission network.
India is not alone in facing these kinds of grid challenges. Trade body SolarPower Europe commented on the situation regarding grid infrastructure in Europe in September this year, saying that “investment in storage, electrification, flexibility and grid infrastructure must scale rapidly.”

climate-energy-7832a67746.fulltext:

India Weighs Agrivoltaics Incentives, Eyes 5 GW In 4 Years
MNRE is considering financial support to help offset higher costs of agrivoltaic projects and reduce competition for land for solar deployment
Key Takeaways
- MNRE is contemplating a support scheme for agrivoltaics either under PM-KUSUM or separately
- The ministry expects India could add around 5 GW of agrivoltaic capacity over the next three to four years
- Financial and policy support could make solar deployment more widespread in the country via agrivoltaics
India is considering a financial support scheme to encourage agrivoltaics to encourage dual use of land for solar power generation and farming. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) sees the potential to add around 5 GW of agrivoltaic capacity over the next three to four years.
MNRE Secretary Santosh Kumar Sarangi recently said that the government was working on a scheme to address the higher costs of agrivoltaic projects and incentivize stated to encourage their adoption. India’s technical agrivoltaics potential currently stands at between 1 TW to 2 TW (see TERI: India’s Agrivoltaic Potential May Reach 2.1 TW).
Under agrivoltaics, solar panels are installed on elevated structures, allowing crops to grow and farming activities to continue beneath them. The approach could help India expand solar power generation while reducing competition between renewable energy projects and agricultural land. Sarangi stressed that this approach could expand solar deployment beyond the top 5 states that currently account for 85% of deployment, to even those with less non-agricultural land.
Sarangi believes that agrivoltaic projects cost around 25% to 30% more than conventional ground-mounted solar installations because of the additional infrastructure needed to elevate the panels. The proposed scheme aims to address this cost difference and make projects more commercially viable.
The projected addition of 5 GW would nevertheless depend partly on state governments introducing suitable feed-in tariffs (FIT), which determine the price paid for electricity generated by these projects.
As per the ministry’s estimates, the cost of power from agrivoltaics plants could range between INR 3.20 to INR 3.30 per kWh, compared with INR 2.80 to INR 3 per kWh for decentralized solar installations under PM-KUSUM.
The ministry is considering whether to include the support under the existing PM-KUSUM scheme or introduce a separate program. It is working with the Ministry of Finance to determine its structure. It is also working on a policy document to guide the development of agrivoltaics and engaging with electricity distribution companies to facilitate power purchases, according to the MNRE Secretary.
Speaking with the media ahead of the Agrivoltaics World Conference 2026 to be held in New Delhi, Sarangi shared that trials conducted with the Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) have helped identify crops suited to agrivoltaic installations across different agro-climatic zones.
While fruits and leafy vegetables had shown encouraging results, the arrangement doesn’t seem to work as well for rice and sugarcane. He identified Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh as states with potential for deployment.
Earlier this year, India approved a new floating PV scheme to target 5 GW capacity, combined with 2-hour energy storage systems (see India Launches 5 GW Floating Solar Scheme With Storage).

global-economics-ab78586d19.fulltext:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has revealed that the India-US trade deal is “incredibly close”, indicating that finalisation is anticipated shortly.
Speaking to Network18, Rubio noted that while he is not directly engaged in the negotiations, which are handled through the trade representative, he has closely monitored the discussions and expects the agreement to materialise in a matter of weeks, not months.
“I’m not personally negotiating it; it’s done through our trade representative, but I know, and I’ve been very involved in watching it happen, that it is something we anticipate seeing in a matter of weeks, not months,” said Rubio.
Elaborating on the meticulous final stages, he highlighted the necessity of absolute precision prior to public announcements to safeguard bilateral ties of such high importance.
“I felt that way before, and with these deals, it’s always important that it would be totally agreed to, every detail of it, before it’s announced because you can’t afford for a relationship of this magnitude to be threatened by announcing a deal and it turning out the deal wasn’t finalised. But it’s incredibly close. I think we are down to some technical details that need to be worked out. Technical details matter because there has to be an agreement; both sides have to agree that the language means the same thing. So, it’s down to that level,” he said.
‘The preponderance of it is good for you’
Addressing queries concerning comparative rates for India alongside other nations, Rubio affirmed that the overarching outcome remains highly advantageous.
“The preponderance of it is good for you. And that’s what we aim to achieve here, and I can’t wait till we do it because we have so many things we can work together on,” Rubio stated.
Rubio stresses importance of exploring India beyond capitals
Commenting on the sheer magnitude and diversity of the nation, the US Secretary of State underscored the necessity of broad exploratory visits rather than confining diplomatic engagements strictly to capitals.
“Well, this is a big country, it’s an important country, and I think like any big country, I say, people, if you want to learn and see what’s happening in the United States, you can’t just go to Washington. You should probably try to go somewhere in the South, maybe somewhere on the West Coast, and you probably need to get to New York, in Chicago. And so, for us, I mean, I don’t pretend that in my time as a Secretary of State I’ll get to see all of India, or learn about every region, but I think it’s important to see a country of this size and magnitude and to learn as much about it as you can,” Rubio remarked.
Mumbai’s role in India-US trade ties
Highlighting the pivotal role of India’s commercial hub, Rubio explained the strategic rationale behind visiting Mumbai during his diplomatic tour.
“Mumbai, in particular, is the financial heart and soul of the country. It’s where so many of the companies that are investing in and with the United States, and who we want to do more trade with, are located. It’s the financial lifeblood of the country. So, it’s logical to come here, and obviously I look forward to coming back and seeing the country again. I told our media earlier today; they were asking why we were here, you know, that media wants us to go to other parts of the world sometimes, not here. I said we actually don’t come here enough if you think about the importance of this relationship. So now, I’m glad I’m here. But I’m glad there’s a congressional delegation in town at the same time, and I know we’ve sent people here. global-economics-b1e8e7d95d.headline: Musk ordered slowdown of Starlink service used by Ukraine's military, WSJ reports

[Text below is The Times of India's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Elon Musk’s 
SpaceX
 has come under scrutiny over reported disruptions to satellite internet services used by Ukrainian forces, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accusing the company of restricting access during the war with Russia.
A report by The Wall Street Journal, citing officials familiar with the matter, said Musk had directed an intentional slowdown of Ukraine’s essential military Starlink network, triggering alarm in Kyiv and leaving the Trump administration bewildered.
US officials, however, have denied ordering any slowdown. Defence secretary Pete Hegseth said Washington had not directed any reduction in the satellite services, while secretary of state Marco Rubio maintained that the White House was not responsible for the reported disruption.
US says it did not order a slowdown
Speaking to reporters, Hegseth said the US military had not instructed any changes to the satellite service used by Ukraine.
"We haven't pulled anything back," Hegseth said. "Nothing's changed from our view. We haven't made any directives or anything like that. And we wish the Ukrainians obviously success."
He said any operational changes or performance adjustments would fall under the satellite provider's contractual terms.
"There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied with," Hegseth added, noting that "that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions."
Rubio also rejected claims that Washington had ordered Starlink's speed to be reduced. He stressed that Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX, whereas Starshield is a separate military-grade system controlled by the US government.
"Starshield is a defence and military product; that is something that the United States military uses. It is not available to Ukraine, and it is under discussion how they want to use it. I don’t know if Zelenskyy knows what he is talking about. In the United States, nobody ordered that Starlink's speed be slowed down. In my understanding, it has been restored. That is Starlink; they were using Starlink. Starshield is in contract with the US military, has nothing to do with Ukraine."
Rubio said Ukraine was seeking access to Starshield for operations inside Russia, but insisted that the reported disruption had nothing to do with the White House.
"Ukraine wants access to Starshield… in order to conduct deep strikes inside Russia. They do not have access to it at this moment. I don’t know what their theory is, but it has nothing to do with the White House. I saw a report the other day; it is categorically false. No one at the White House ordered the slowdown of the internet so certain drones couldn’t use it," he added.
Zelenskyy alleges disruption affected military operations
The controversy follows concerns over satellite connectivity disruptions that reportedly affected Ukrainian military operations as Russian attacks continued. According to Axios, Zelenskyy raised concerns about the impact of the disruptions on Ukraine's ability to defend itself.
In an interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan on Piers Morgan Uncensored, Zelenskyy accused Musk of restricting Ukrainian access to Starlink and said the disruption had affected military operations.
"I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely," Zelenskyy said, referring to the reported disruption.
"Because it was 1 am at night, (when) Starlink was blocked by SpaceX and the United States," he added.
CNN reported that Ukrainian authorities were caught off guard by restrictions affecting Starshield. A Ukrainian military source with direct knowledge of the impact told the broadcaster, "The complications are substantial."
Ukrainian forces rely on Starlink connectivity to operate reconnaissance and interceptor drones, gather intelligence and carry out other battlefield activities. Any disruption to the service can therefore affect communications and the coordination of military operations.
Starlink connectivity reportedly being restored
Mykhailo Fedorov, former minister of defence of Ukraine, later said Starlink connectivity was being restored and called for the removal of restrictions affecting Starshield.
"Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h is being restored. Removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defence. Thank you, Elon Musk. We hope for your continued support," Fedorov posted on X.
The dispute highlights Ukraine's reliance on satellite communications for its war effort and the influence that private technology providers can have on military operations. While US officials deny ordering a slowdown, questions remain over the reported disruption, the distinction between Starlink and Starshield, and the terms under which Ukraine can access these services.

work-careers-ac30b99df9.fulltext:
A growing number of tech workers from India are leaving the U.S. to return home, according to a report by The Economic Times. Around 12,700 professionals had made the move by September 2026, putting the year on track to surpass last year’s record of 15,100, according to data from Xpheno.
The numbers have risen steadily in recent years, increasing from 7,200 in 2023 to 9,800 in 2024. If the trend continues, India could soon see more tech professionals returning from the U.S. rather than moving there.
READ: As EB-1 advances for Indians, experts break down the October visa bulletin (October 4, 2026)
The trend comes amid growing uncertainty over immigration and visa policies under the Trump administration. Rising layoffs and limited stability in global hiring have also contributed to the shift.
LinkedIn member Abhinarayan Mishra noted that returning to India does not guarantee an “easy landing.” According to Mishra, Indian employers are prioritizing expertise in artificial intelligence, cloud computing, cybersecurity and product leadership over general international experience. He also pointed to tax compliance requirements in both the U.S. and India, as well as potential education and adjustment challenges for returning professionals’ Gen Z children.
The trend comes after the suspension of PERM processing for some of the largest recruiters of global talent, including Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys, Cognizant, Capgemini, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Tata.
PERM, or Program Electronic Review Management, is a key step in the employer-sponsored green card process. It generally requires employers to demonstrate that there are not enough qualified, available U.S. workers for a position and that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed American workers.
For Indian professionals relying on employer sponsorship, the suspension could delay their plans to obtain permanent residency. The impact, however, will depend on their current immigration status and the stage of their green card applications.
According to immigration expert Swatilina Barik, the action does not cancel existing H-1B visas or affect green cards that have already been approved. Instead, it prevents the affected companies from filing new PERM applications and pauses pending applications while the suspension remains in effect. Barik said the development should be understood as a restriction on the employment-based permanent residency pathway rather than a cancellation of temporary work authorization.

Rules governing H-1B visas are also facing potential changes. U.S. companies that violate H-1B rules could face fines of up to $250,000 and bans from federal immigration programs lasting as long as 10 years under a bill introduced in Congress.
The H-1B Visa Fraud Crackdown Act, introduced Oct. 1 by Republican Rep. Beth Van Duyne of Texas, would significantly increase penalties for employers that intentionally violate H-1B rules. The proposal would also authorize the government to bar certain companies from participating in immigration programs for up to 10 years.

global-economics-6e17a876f9.headline: Billionaire Mukesh Ambani launches India’s biggest-ever IPO
global-economics-6e17a876f9.fulltext:
India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.
Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.
Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.
Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.
On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.
Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.
The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.
At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.
However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.
It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.
Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.
Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.
“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”

ai-c723746d1e.headline: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems
ai-c723746d1e.fulltext:
The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, and covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions.
The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from U.S. government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said.
The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the U.S. and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models.
China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to an official briefing. “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added.
The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems.
Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week.
The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the globe since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off of Nvidia shares.
The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to a September report.
In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. agritech-6d41aa77de.headline: India-New Zealand FTA kicks in: Zero duty, more opportunities - what's in it for India?
agritech-6d41aa77de.fulltext:
NEW DELHI: The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) came into force on Tuesday opening up new opportunities for Indian exporters, manufacturers, farmers, professionals and businesses. The agreement provides 100% duty-free access to the New Zealand market for all Indian export tariff lines, removing peak tariffs of up to 10%.
Signed on April 27, 2026, the pact aims to deepen economic ties between the two countries and double bilateral trade in goods and services to NZ$7 billion (Rs 35,000 crore) by 2030. Negotiations were launched on March 16, 2025, and concluded on December 22, 2025, within nine months.
The agreement is India's 17th operational FTA and the seventh trade pact to come into force in the past five years. It covers goods, services, investment, agriculture, skills and mobility, while retaining safeguards for sensitive sectors.
What's in it for India?
1. Duty-free access for Indian exporters
All Indian goods can enter New Zealand duty-free, giving Indian exporters a competitive advantage and placing them on a level playing field with New Zealand's other FTA partners. 
Textiles, apparel, leather, footwear, gems and jewellery, engineering goods, automobiles and auto components, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, agricultural products and processed foods are among the sectors expected to benefit.
Duty-free access for wooden logs, coking coal and metal waste and scrap will strengthen manufacturing and MSME supply chains. Streamlined regulatory processes are expected to benefit pharmaceutical and medical device industries.
2. A boost for MSMEs and small businesses
The agreement opens New Zealand's market to micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), women-led businesses, start-ups, artisans and first-generation entrepreneurs.
Zero duties and faster customs processes are expected to reduce landed costs and help Indian businesses expand their customer base. Cooperation will improve access to trade-related information and links with New Zealand's small and medium enterprise ecosystem, with particular attention to businesses owned by women and young people.
New Zealand has also committed to facilitating the registration of Indian geographical indications (GIs), creating opportunities to protect products associated with rural artisans and traditional industries.
3. New opportunities for farmers
The Agricultural Productivity Partnership will bring technology, training and global best practices to Indian agriculture, extending cooperation beyond tariff concessions.
Dedicated action plans for apples, kiwifruit and honey will support better orchard management, reduce post-harvest losses and improve productivity and farm incomes. Cooperation will also cover horticulture, forestry, livestock and fisheries.
New Zealand will provide technical assistance to establish Centres of Excellence for kiwifruit, apples and honey. Phase I sites for kiwifruit centres have been identified at Pfutsero in Nagaland and Magra in Uttarakhand. Two apple centres are proposed in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, while honey centres are envisaged in Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal.
Tariff rate quotas for apples, kiwifruit and Mānuka honey are linked to the delivery of action plans and overseen by a Joint Agriculture Productivity Council, linking market access with farmer welfare.
4. More opportunities for Indian professionals and students
New Zealand has offered market access in around 118 services sectors and Most-Favoured-Nation commitments in about 139 sub-sectors, its most extensive services offered under any trade agreement to date.
For the first time, dedicated access has been provided for health and traditional medicine services, including Ayurveda, yoga and other AYUSH systems.
Indian youth and professionals will have access to 5,000 Temporary Employment Entry visas and 1,000 Working Holiday visas annually.
There will be no numerical cap on Indian students. Post-study work rights will extend to three years for STEM bachelor's and master's graduates and up to four years for doctoral scholars.
5. Investment, manufacturing and employment
New Zealand has committed to facilitating $20 billion in investment into India over more than 15 years.
The investment is expected to benefit agriculture, manufacturing, infrastructure and start-ups, supporting innovation, entrepreneurship and employment generation under the Make in India vision.
Provisions covering duty-free inputs, bilateral cumulation, customs facilitation and investment promotion could encourage deeper integration into value chains and improve investment conditions.
6. Safeguards for sensitive Indian sectors
Dairy, sugar, edible oils and key agricultural commodities remain excluded from concessions to protect farmers, dairy producers, fisherfolk and rural communities.
Rules of Origin, a bilateral safeguard mechanism and anti-circumvention provisions aim to ensure that benefits reach genuine Indian exporters.
7. A larger trade partnership
Bilateral trade fell about 11% to $1.15 billion in 2025-26, from $1.3 billion in the previous fiscal year. India's exports stood at $566.51 million, while imports were $589.1 million, leaving a trade deficit of $22.59 million.
The FTA seeks to reverse the limited scale of trade and expand economic engagement. The first-ever export of a JCB machine from India to New Zealand was flagged off at the entry-into-force ceremony, with further product flag-offs planned across agriculture, gems and jewellery, engineering, sporting goods, footwear and leather.
Commerce minister Piyush Goyal said that the agreement would create opportunities for exporters, particularly MSMEs, artisans, farmers and women entrepreneurs. The pact also supports India's strategic partnership with New Zealand and the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047, with its success ultimately depending on businesses converting improved market access into actual trade and investment.
