India-New Zealand FTA opens duty-free export opportunities for startups
India’s consumer brands, agri-businesses and manufacturing startups could get a boost in overseas expansion as a new free trade agreement (FTA) with New Zealand removes tariffs on Indian goods, giving exporters duty-free access to a market where several product categories have so far had a limited foothold.
The agreement, which takes effect on October 20, also comes with a commitment by New Zealand to facilitate $20 billion in investment into India, raising the prospect of fresh capital for domestic businesses.
Under the India-New Zealand FTA, Indian exports will receive zero-duty access across all tariff lines, eliminating peak tariffs of up to 10 per cent.
“Ours is a winning partnership, both on and off the field,” Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal said in a statement.
The two governments have also outlined cooperation in agriculture, including technical assistance to improve productivity and reduce post-harvest losses. For startups in these sectors, duty-free access could improve price competitiveness in New Zealand.
A market beyond India
The opportunity comes as Indian consumer businesses seek to diversify beyond the domestic market.
According to government data, in the fiscal year 2024-25, India exported a total of $2.5 billion worth of footwear worldwide, including $2.28 million to New Zealand. Leather exports amounted to $3.08 billion globally, with $6.23 million directed to New Zealand. Additionally, gems and jewellery exports reached $29.96 billion worldwide, of which $16.91 million was sent to New Zealand.
Goyal said the agreement would create opportunities across agriculture, gems and jewellery, engineering, sporting goods, footwear and leather. “These initiatives reflect the confidence of Indian manufacturers and the opportunities the agreement opens up for exporters across the country,” he said, referring to planned product export flag-offs marking the agreement’s implementation.
Additionally, the Bharati programme, a flagship initiative launched by the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority, selected 100 agri-food startups in 2026 for export-focused training.
The FTA provides for New Zealand’s technical assistance through centres of excellence for certain consumer goods to improve farm productivity and reduce post-harvest losses, creating potential opportunities for Indian agritech, food-processing and supply-chain startups, alongside broader manufacturing opportunities linked to the $20 billion investment commitment.
The agreement would also strengthen access to trade-related information and business networks, including links with New Zealand’s small-business ecosystem, with particular attention to enterprises owned by women and young entrepreneurs.

work-careers-17a9395aa2.headline: India-New Zealand FTA opens 5,000 temporary work visa slots for Indians
work-careers-17a9395aa2.fulltext:
India-New Zealand FTA opens 5,000 temporary work visa slots for Indians
The pact covers IT, engineering, healthcare and education professionals, with eligible workers allowed to stay for up to three years
Listen to This Article
India’s free trade agreement (FTA) with New Zealand, effective October 20, creates a new temporary work visa pathway for skilled Indian professionals, with a quota of 5,000 visas at any given time and stays of up to three years.
The pathway covers sectors such as information technology (IT), engineering, construction, education and healthcare. It also includes certain Indian occupations, including yoga instructors, chefs, music teachers and Ayush practitioners.
The agreement also provides temporary entry arrangements for business visitors, professionals supplying contractual services and employees transferred within the same company. The provisions are intended to improve access to New Zealand’s market for Indian service providers, according to PTI.
Which professionals can benefit?
The agreement provides different permitted stays depending on the nature of the work.
Skilled professionals: The new temporary employment entry pathway has a quota of 5,000 visas at any given time, allowing eligible applicants to stay for up to three years.
Also Read
Intra-company transferees: Employees transferred within the same company can stay for up to three years.
Contractual service providers and independent professionals: Eligible professionals can stay for up to 12 months.
Business visitors and equipment specialists: Business visitors and workers installing or servicing equipment can stay for up to 90 days in a 12-month period.
These provisions do not mean that every Indian applicant will automatically qualify for a visa. Eligibility will depend on the applicable requirements and the category under which the person seeks entry.
The FTA creates a structured route for certain professionals to work or visit New Zealand for specific periods. However, the temporary employment pathway should not be confused with permanent residency or an automatic route to citizenship.
Services sector gets wider market access
New Zealand has agreed to open 118 services sectors or sub-sectors to Indian service providers under the pact. These include IT, professional services, telecommunications, construction, education, financial services and tourism.
The wider access could create opportunities for Indian companies and professionals seeking business in New Zealand. The temporary entry provisions may also help eligible workers undertake assignments, provide specialised services or move within multinational companies.
The actual benefits will depend on how businesses use the agreement and whether professionals meet the relevant entry conditions.
What the trade pact aims to achieve
The agreement came into force at 12:01 am on October 20 in India. It is designed to expand trade in goods and services, improve market access and encourage investment between the two countries.
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said the pact aims to increase bilateral trade in goods and services from about $2.4 billion to around 7 billion New Zealand dollars, or approximately Rs 35,000 crore, by 2030, PTI reported.
For Indian exporters, New Zealand has offered zero-duty access across all tariff lines, covering 100 per cent of India’s current exports to the country. The agreement also envisages $20 billion in foreign direct investment from New Zealand into India over the next 15 years.
For Indian professionals, however, the main benefit is the creation of a defined temporary entry pathway and expanded services-sector access. Those considering opportunities in New Zealand should check the eligibility conditions for their occupation and visa category before making employment or relocation plans.

New Zealand is giving 100% duty-free market access to Indian exporters from Tuesday (October 20, 2026). It covers all tariff lines or product categories and 100% of India’s current exports to New Zealand.

india-44e522cb49.headline: India-US trade deal expected in weeks, says Marco Rubio
india-44e522cb49.fulltext:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has revealed that the India-US trade deal is “incredibly close”, indicating that finalisation is anticipated shortly.
Speaking to Network18, Rubio noted that while he is not directly engaged in the negotiations, which are handled through the trade representative, he has closely monitored the discussions and expects the agreement to materialise in a matter of weeks, not months.
“I’m not personally negotiating it; it’s done through our trade representative, but I know, and I’ve been very involved in watching it happen, that it is something we anticipate seeing in a matter of weeks, not months,” said Rubio.
Elaborating on the meticulous final stages, he highlighted the necessity of absolute precision prior to public announcements to safeguard bilateral ties of such high importance.
“I felt that way before, and with these deals, it’s always important that it would be totally agreed to, every detail of it, before it’s announced because you can’t afford for a relationship of this magnitude to be threatened by announcing a deal and it turning out the deal wasn’t finalised. But it’s incredibly close. I think we are down to some technical details that need to be worked out. Technical details matter because there has to be an agreement; both sides have to agree that the language means the same thing. So, it’s down to that level,” he said.
‘The preponderance of it is good for you’
Addressing queries concerning comparative rates for India alongside other nations, Rubio affirmed that the overarching outcome remains highly advantageous.
“The preponderance of it is good for you. And that’s what we aim to achieve here, and I can’t wait till we do it because we have so many things we can work together on,” Rubio stated.
Rubio stresses importance of exploring India beyond capitals
Commenting on the sheer magnitude and diversity of the nation, the US Secretary of State underscored the necessity of broad exploratory visits rather than confining diplomatic engagements strictly to capitals.
“Well, this is a big country, it’s an important country, and I think like any big country, I say, people, if you want to learn and see what’s happening in the United States, you can’t just go to Washington. You should probably try to go somewhere in the South, maybe somewhere on the West Coast, and you probably need to get to New York, in Chicago. And so, for us, I mean, I don’t pretend that in my time as a Secretary of State I’ll get to see all of India, or learn about every region, but I think it’s important to see a country of this size and magnitude and to learn as much about it as you can,” Rubio remarked.
Mumbai’s role in India-US trade ties
Highlighting the pivotal role of India’s commercial hub, Rubio explained the strategic rationale behind visiting Mumbai during his diplomatic tour.
“Mumbai, in particular, is the financial heart and soul of the country. It’s where so many of the companies that are investing in and with the United States, and who we want to do more trade with, are located. It’s the financial lifeblood of the country. So, it’s logical to come here, and obviously I look forward to coming back and seeing the country again. I told our media earlier today; they were asking why we were here, you know, that media wants us to go to other parts of the world sometimes, not here. I said we actually don’t come here enough if you think about the importance of this relationship. So now, I’m glad I’m here. But I’m glad there’s a congressional delegation in town at the same time, and I know we’ve sent people here. The Attorney General’s been here, the Commerce Secretary’s been here, and I expect to be back,” he added.

india-cd50a1bef4.headline: "We're About As Close As You Can Be": Marco Rubio On India-US Trade Deal
india-cd50a1bef4.fulltext:
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar hosted Rubio for wide-ranging talks shortly after the top diplomat arrived in Mumbai for his second visit to India in under five months, even as bilateral ties remain strained over Washington's unpredictable trade policies and tightening immigration rules.
India and the US moved to expand energy and defence cooperation on Tuesday despite ongoing friction in their relations, as Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged New Delhi to scale up energy trade and increase the purchase of American technologies and systems.
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar hosted Rubio for wide-ranging talks shortly after the top diplomat arrived in Mumbai for his second visit to India in under five months, even as bilateral ties remain strained over Washington's unpredictable trade policies and tightening immigration rules.
Ahead of his meeting with Jaishankar, Rubio told the media that the India-US trade deal is close to finalisation. He also described India as a crude oil refining "superpower" and advocated for processing more Venezuelan crude in India. The Secretary of State is scheduled to visit Reliance Industries Ltd-owned Jamnagar Refinery on Wednesday.
Rubio, answering a question on the trade pact, said that " a small number of items" are left to be wrapped up and hoped that it will be sealed "shortly".
"I would say we're about as close as you can be without having an executed agreement. I think there's a small number of items left to wrap up. So I think that will happen shortly -- we're hoping, which it should -- and hopefully have some good news to announce fairly soon. And perhaps the leaders can sign it thereafter," he said.
Following the meeting, Jaishankar said on social media that he and Rubio "shared views on further advancement of our ties, focusing on trade, energy, technology, defence and people-to-people ties." The US State Department said the secretary and the external affairs minister discussed regional and global issues, including developments in West Asia.
"The secretary reiterated that increased energy trade with the United States can play a transformative role in diversifying India's supply chains while meeting its sizable consumer demand," it said.
"He also commended recent progress in bilateral defense and civil nuclear cooperation, and advocated for the increased purchase of US technologies and systems, which can enhance the security and prosperity of both our countries," the State Department added.
Before his talks with Jaishankar, Rubio visited the Taj memorial and laid a wreath in honour of the victims of the horrific 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks that included six American citizens.
"In Mumbai, Indian External Affairs Minister @DrSJaishankar and I discussed energy security and defense cooperation while reaffirming the importance of advancing the U.S.-India strategic partnership," Rubio said on 'X'.
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said Rubio and Jaishankar had "productive discussions" on deepening US-India cooperation across defence, energy, emerging technologies, and trade, as "we continue to build the unrivalled momentum in our bilateral partnership." The envoy was also present at the meeting.
In his brief media interaction, Rubio also responded to a question on whether the US administration was upset with New Delhi over the amount of Russian oil it procured last year and its efforts to reduce the volume.
"I think what India has expressed repeatedly is its desire to diversify their energy portfolio, which is a smart thing to do. Obviously, it's not easy to do that from one day to the next day," he said.
"I think they've made substantial progress in that regard, and we're happy to see that. But in the end, it's not just about Russian oil; it's about their desire to diversify, and obviously we think we can be a source of some of their energy inputs."
"Obviously, We've discussed Venezuela and other countries, and I think it's in our interest to have a strong ally with a diverse energy portfolio," he said.
The US Secretary of State also hailed India's oil refining capabilities. "India is a refining superpower. They have the ability to do that and they have companies that know how to do that."
Rubio also pointed out that certain Indian companies have "pre-existing oil concessions in Venezuela".
"I'm not claiming to you that Venezuela alone can fill the hole that could be caused by some of the things that are happening around the world, but I think over time, it most certainly can, and in the short term, it can certainly provide the means," he said.
"So, that's one of the things we'll talk about. With India, we've talked about it in the past, and they sound ready. They're ready to do it; they're willing to do it," he noted.
The top diplomat also answered a question on his trip to Reliance Industries Ltd's refinery in Jamnagar on Wednesday.
"Energy is related to national security. Countries fight wars over energy, economies collapse over lack of energy. We're going to go see a company that has a tremendous amount of refining capability. It makes all the sense in the world to talk to them about it," he said.
During the media interaction, Rubio said several geopolitical developments, including the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi attacks on energy pipelines in Saudi Arabia, impacted energy supplies, causing several countries to grapple with a diesel shortage.
Last week, US President Donald Trump suspended certain sanctions against Russia and five of the biggest buyers of Russian oil including India. He also announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release hundreds of thousands of tonnes of Russian diesel onto the world market.
Rubio and Jaishankar also laid a wreath at the 26/11 memorial at the Hotel Taj to honour the victims of the terror attack.
"We must continue our strong partnership in combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations," Jaishankar said in a social media post.
"At the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, I laid a wreath honoring the victims of the horrific November 26, 2008 terrorist attacks, including six American citizens," Rubio said.
"We remember those lost, honour the courage of those who responded, and reaffirm the enduring US-India partnership and our shared commitment to combating terrorism," he added.
Jaishankar, addressing a reception celebrating 250 Years of American Independence, said Indian talent and Indian skills have helped "shape the tech era in the US".
"Of course, we've had our share of issues, including the manner in which we approach the world and its challenges. But in the last few decades, our partnership has steadily expanded, acquiring new dimensions and new facets," he said.
Jaishankar also underlined the importance of deeper India-US ties when the world order is "clearly in transition and countries are responding accordingly".
"Each one of us will naturally pursue our national interest. In such an era, expanding our convergence is key to deepening our ties."
"There are new opportunities in our partnership, in trade, investment, technology and energy, and these await us. We have a shared stake in strengthening peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific," he added.
India-US relations witnessed a major downturn after Washington imposed punitive tariffs on India last year and President Trump made assertions regarding his role in de-escalating the India-Pakistan military clashes of May 2025 that drew sharp reaction from Indian officials.
Washington's new immigration policy and its decision to increase the H1B visa fee also contributed to the slide in India-US ties.
The ties came under fresh strain after the US decided to restrict a key green-card processing programme for major global and Indian IT firms, including Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro.
